newsitem.title: USA: xxxxTobacco firms defend settlement, warn against delay.
newsitem.headline: xxxxTobacco firms defend settlement, warn against delay.

text.p: Tobacco industry representatives Thursday defended a $368.5 billion settlement and warned it could be lost if Congress and the White House dallied over changes, the Washington Post reported Friday.

The newspaper said two industry representatives met with a small group of reporters, rebutting criticism of the most controversial elements of the landmark deal, including a provision restricting the federal government's ability to regulate nicotine.

One of the industry representatives, both of whom spoke on condition that they not be named, said the agreement made it "possible to have solutions to some of these problems that are just not achievable" without a negotiated settlement, according to the Post.
"It's not perfect, but it's far better than what the alternatives are," the representative said.

The officials said the provision that limits the Food and Drug Administration's ability to regulate nicotine was "critical" to the industry and part of a package that could be undone by too much tinkering.
They said other provisions gave the agency "powerful tools" to drive the companies to produce safer products and were preferable to heavy-handed regulation of nicotine.

Under the proposed settlement, the industry would pay $368.5 billion over 25 years and curtail advertising and marketing. Some of the money would go to anti-smoking programmes and reimburse states for treating patients with diseases related to smoking.
The agreement is being reviewed by Congress and a presidential task force.
One source told the paper he did not see room for further compromise on limits on class action lawsuits, another provision that has been criticised.
